extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic/metaphysics; philosophers and philosophy students
extracted.subtask_description: Provide logical/metaphysical criteria for classifying the kinds of things that names denote (substances, attributes — qualities/quantities/relations — bodies, minds), and for analyzing what grounds those attributes and relations. The guidance is aimed at analytic treatment of terms in logic rather than metaphysical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-logicians' distinction between attribute and substance
rubrics_metrics.description: An attribute must be the attribute of something (e.g., colour must be the colour of something), while a substance is self-existent and need not be followed by 'of' after its name (e.g., 'a stone' is simply 'the stone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: colour, goodness (attributes) vs. stone, moon (substances). Notes and caveats: the account depends on understanding the particle 'of' and on the idea of self-existence; the text highlights problems with taking this distinction at face value (see the critique entry). Use this as the classical/logical school formulation when classifying ordinary language usages, but be aware of counterexamples (relative names like 'father') and conceptual difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of the simple attribute/substance test
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'attribute if it is of something, substance if self-existent' test is defective: relative/subordinate names (e.g., 'father') blur the divide, and attributes and substances are mutually interdependent since one cannot conceive a substance without attributes nor attributes without some subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'father' must be father of something (resembles an attribute) yet the man could exist though the child were annihilated; destroy all white substances and 'whiteness' would be a contradiction. Guidance: do not rely solely on the grammatical test ('of' after a name) or on naive self-existence; deeper analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Body (received doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Body may be defined as 'the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations' — an external something, independent of the mind and bodily organs, considered as the cause of sensory states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the standard metaphysical/logical definition when treating 'body' as the presumed external cause of grouped sensations. Examples: sensations of yellow, hardness, weight when handling gold are ascribed to the body. Application: when analysing talk about physical objects, treat 'body' as the hypothesised cause behind recurring bundles of sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealist/phenomenalist account of Body (set-of-sensations view)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative account holds that a body is nothing intrinsically different from the sensations it is said to produce; it is a set of sensations joined together according to a fixed law (i.e., bodies = complexes of sensations bound by regular connexions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view is illustrated by the thought-experiment of annihilating a substratum yet allowing sensations to continue: if sensations and their lawful connexion remain, the substratum would be undetectable. Use this criterion when adopting an anti-realist/phenomenalist analysis of physical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic/intuitive defence of belief in external bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reply to the idealist: belief in matter is intuitive; humans are compelled by nature to refer sensations to an external cause, and in practice we behave as if bodies exist even if theoretical sceptics deny them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the common-sense/logical rationale for treating bodies as external causes in ordinary and scientific discourse. It marks a methodological stance: for logic, accept the positing of external cause as an intuitive premise rather than prove it by extrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Mind is conceived as 'an unknown recipient, or percipient' of sensations and all other feelings; the thinking principle is known only through the 'thread of consciousness' — a series of feelings (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing mental terms, treat 'mind' as the subject which has or feels the series of states of consciousness. Emphasize epistemic limits: we know only the states, not the inmost nature of the thinking principle itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological limit: we know only sensations and their order
rubrics_metrics.description: All we can know of objects is the sensations they give us and the order in which those sensations occur; the real nature ('thing in itself') of objects is effectively unknowable by our faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a foundational constraint for logical analysis of names: restrict proofs and definitions to observable sensations and their relations rather than claims about intrinsic natures. Cites Kant, Berkeley, Locke as agreeing on this point for the purposes of logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes classified into Quality, Quantity, Relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes (what names denote beyond substances) are customarily distributed under three heads: Quality, Quantity, and Relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or categorizing attributes of named things, first assign them to one of these three classes; subsequent analysis proceeds differently for each class (the chapter develops Quality then Relation here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality grounded on sensations (foundation of quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality ascribed to an object (e.g., whiteness) is grounded upon the sensation which the object's presence excites in us; the 'sensation' is termed the 'foundation' of the quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two views exist: (a) qualities are nothing but the sensations (recommended for logic), (b) qualities are powers inherent in objects producing sensations. For logical purposes adopt language compatible with either, but treat the sensation as the essential part: proving the sensation proves the quality. Example: whiteness = the sensation of white colour; proving that snow excites that sensation suffices to prove it has the quality whiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid positing occult or superfluous causes for qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unnecessary (and logically sterile) to posit an additional occult 'virtue' or power beyond the fact that the object produces the sensation; saying 'opium has a soporific virtue' is merely restating the observed fact that opium puts to sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an anti-pattern: do not explain a quality by inventing an unobservable entity ('virtue') that merely rephrases the observed effect. Prefer parsimonious analysis that ties attributes to observable regularities of sensation and to the known causal chain, however much the ultimate mechanism remains inexplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation defined by fundamentum relationis
rubrics_metrics.description: A Relation is an attribute grounded upon some fact or phenomenon into which the object enters jointly with one or more other objects; the common fact is the 'fundamentum relationis' (the foundation of the relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To analyze a relational term, identify the specific fact (series of facts, or states of consciousness) in which the two related things jointly participate. Examples: greater/less (one covers the other when applied), master/servant (one undertakes services for another), husband/wife (legal/formal facts and consequences). The fundamentum may often be resolvable into states of consciousness (intentions, acts, sensations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal relations as fundamenta (antecedent/consequent, simultaneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple relations of antecedence, consequence, and simultaneity are grounded in the succession or simultaneity of sensations; e.g., 'dawn preceded sunrise' is grounded in the successive sensations constituting our consciousness of those events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse temporal relational claims by examining the order of sensations or experiences. Note the chapter's point that succession/simultaneity are not additional 'third things' but conditions involved in having two feelings at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance/likeness grounded in sensations plus a feeling of resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemblance (likeness) and unlikeness are relations constituted by two sensations and the observer's feeling of resemblance (or lack thereof); resemblance itself is a state of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing claims of similarity, include both the underlying sensations (e.g., two colour sensations) and the psychological state (feeling) that registers resemblance. Consider whether the feeling of resemblance is an additional state or is involved in the original sensations analogously to succession.
